blocks.text: Two main groups of proteins take part in the non-specific defence of the body.

Proteins made in the liver form the complement system: more than a dozen proteins that circulate in the blood in an inactive state. On meeting a microbe they become active in a sequence, the first activating the second and so on. The final five proteins form a membrane-attack complex (MAC) in the microbe's plasma membrane, which punctures it; fluids and salts move in, and the microbe swells and bursts.

blocks.alt: Five yellow circles C1 to C5 joined by arrows show complement proteins activating one another in sequence. An arrow leads to a microbe's membrane in which a ring of yellow proteins, the membrane-attack complex, forms a pore; a blue arrow shows fluids and salts rushing in.
blocks.caption: The complement cascade and the membrane-attack complex (original diagram after Figure 21.7).
blocks.long_description: Proteins made in the liver form the complement system: more than a dozen proteins that circulate in the blood in an inactive state. On meeting a microbe they become active in sequence, the first activating the second and so on. The final five proteins form a membrane-attack complex (MAC) in the microbe's plasma membrane, which punctures it, so fluids and salts move in and the microbe swells and bursts.

blocks.text: Interferons are protective proteins released by virus-infected cells. They cause nearby cells to strengthen their anti-viral defences. Interferons belong to the large class of cytokines, proteins that work in communication between cells to trigger the protective defences of the immune system, and they also activate other immune cells such as natural killer cells and macrophages.

blocks.alt: A virus-infected cell on the left containing virus particles releases a trail of small teal interferon molecules. An arrow leads to a neighbouring cell with receptors on its surface, labelled as boosting its anti-viral defences.
blocks.caption: Interferon alerting a neighbouring cell (original diagram after Figure 21.8).
blocks.long_description: Interferons are protective proteins released by virus-infected cells. They make nearby cells strengthen their anti-viral defences. Interferons belong to the large class of cytokines, proteins that carry signals between cells to trigger the protective defences of the immune system, and they also activate other immune cells such as natural killer cells and macrophages.
